find: In the 1960s, Goldthorpe and Lockwood had studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton, arguing that affluent workers were becoming <dfn class="term" data-def="The process by which the working class is said to adopt the attitudes, values and lifestyle of the middle class as their incomes rise.">embourgeoisified</dfn> — absorbed into middle-class values and lifestyles as wages rose.
replace: In the 1960s, Goldthorpe and Lockwood studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton to test the claim that affluent workers were becoming <dfn class="term" data-def="The process by which the working class is said to adopt the attitudes, values and lifestyle of the middle class as their incomes rise.">embourgeoisified</dfn> — absorbed into middle-class values and lifestyles as wages rose. They rejected that claim. The workers kept a separate working-class outlook.
note: F1: Goldthorpe and Lockwood tested and rejected embourgeoisement; the lesson credited them with the thesis they disproved.

find: Weber’s three types of authority are all forms of <dfn class="term" data-def="Power exercised through official institutions, laws or constitutional offices, backed by formal rules and often sanctioned by the state.">formal power</dfn> — power that operates through official channels and recognised institutions. But power is also exercised informally.
replace: Traditional and rational-legal authority usually work as <dfn class="term" data-def="Power exercised through official institutions, laws or constitutional offices, backed by formal rules and often sanctioned by the state.">formal power</dfn> — power that operates through official channels and recognised institutions. Charismatic authority often works outside those channels, because it rests on the leader rather than on an office. Power is also exercised informally.
note: F4: charismatic authority rests on the person, not on an office, so it is not a form of formal power.

find: The mark scheme expects: the correct name (1 mark), the source of legitimacy explained (1 mark), and a developed example (1 mark).
replace: A secure answer names the type, then explains what makes that form of authority legitimate and gives an example. The name on its own will not reach full marks.
note: F5: removes an invented per-mark breakdown that also contradicted this lesson's own practice keys.

find: Fiona Devine’s return to Luton to revisit workers first studied by Goldthorpe and Lockwood is an example of a longitudinal research design: by comparing findings at two points in time, she was able to assess whether class experiences had changed.
replace: Fiona Devine’s return to Luton is a restudy rather than a true longitudinal design. She interviewed a fresh sample of workers in the same town and compared her findings with the earlier study by Goldthorpe and Lockwood. A restudy shows change over time without following the same people.
note: F6: Devine did not track the same individuals, so the study is a restudy, not longitudinal.

note: F7: the CSEW sample is about 31,000 adults and 1,500 children, not 50,000 households.

expect: An annual victim survey of around 50,000 households asking whether they have been victims of crime, regardless of police reporting.
value: An annual victim survey of about 30,000 adults, asking whether they have been victims of crime, whether or not they told the police.
